problemText: A dot plot shows data on a number line where each value in a data set gets its own dot. What happens when the same value appears more than once in the data set?
choices: The dots are stacked directly on top of each other above that value.
The dots are placed side by side horizontally next to each other.
Only one dot is drawn, no matter how many times the value appears.
The value is combined with nearby values and shown as a single mark.
hints: Think about what happens to multiple pets at the same number on Ms. Rivera's plot.
The key word is 'stack'—dots are placed vertically, not horizontally.

problemText: A teacher collects data on the number of books read by 8 students: 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 4. If this data is displayed as a dot plot, how many dots would be stacked above the value 2?
choices: 2 dots
3 dots
4 dots
8 dots
hints: Count how many times the value 2 appears in the list.
Remember that each occurrence of 2 gets its own dot, stacked above that value.

problemText: A histogram displays data with intervals that are all the same width. Why do the bars in a histogram sit directly next to each other with no gaps between them?
choices: Because gaps would make the histogram look cluttered and interrupt the visual flow showing how data is distributed across intervals.
Because histograms must follow a formatting rule that distinguishes them from other graph types used in mathematics and statistics.
Because each value belongs to exactly one interval, and the bars represent consecutive, non-overlapping intervals.
Because the number line must be completely filled to show all possible values without leaving any empty space.
hints: Think about what happens if two intervals overlap or if there is a gap between them.
Every single data value needs to fit into exactly one interval—no value can be counted twice or left out.

problemText: A coach collects data from 25 players on how many goals they scored. The values range from 3 goals all the way to 48 goals, and most players scored a different number. The coach wants to display this data on a single page that is easy to read. Should the coach use a dot plot or a histogram, and what is the main reason?
choices: A dot plot, because it can display any amount of data and makes every individual score visible so nothing gets hidden in intervals.
A histogram, because histograms are more professional and work for any data set no matter the size.
A dot plot, because 25 values is a small data set and small data sets always use dot plots.
A histogram, because there are many values spread across a wide range, and grouping them into intervals keeps the display readable.
hints: Look at the size of the data set (25) and how spread out the values are (3 to 48).
Compare this situation to Mr. Okafor's 20 homework-minutes data—what made a histogram a good choice there?

problemText: A histogram shows how many hours 16 students spent studying for a test. The intervals are 0-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-11 hours. The bars have heights of 4, 6, 4, and 2 respectively. A student looks at the bar above the 6-8 interval and says, 'This bar tells me that 4 students studied for exactly 7 hours.' Why is this statement incorrect?
choices: Because the bar only tells us that 4 students studied somewhere between 6 and 8 hours, not that all of them studied exactly 7 hours.
Because the interval 6-8 contains more than 4 specific values that could be scored, so grouping them loses information about which exact values actually occurred.
Because histograms record frequencies in ranges rather than exact measurements, and 4 students somewhere in that interval could have studied 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, or 8 hours separately.
Because the bar height represents a frequency count across an entire interval, not the number of students who chose one particular value within that range.
hints: Think about what is lost when individual values are grouped into an interval.
A histogram groups data together for readability—what exact information is no longer visible once values are grouped?

problemText: A teacher displays student test scores on a histogram with equal intervals: 60-69, 70-79, 80-89, and 90-99. The bar heights are 3, 7, 8, and 2 respectively. The teacher then decides to create a dot plot of the same data. What would be a valid concern about making this switch from a histogram to a dot plot?
choices: A dot plot cannot show scores in the 60-69 range because those are too low to measure accurately.
The dot plot would need 20 dots spread across 40 possible exact values, and if students actually scored many different exact scores, the plot could become crowded and hard to read.
A dot plot is not allowed if there are more than 15 data points because the display rules require switching to intervals for larger data sets.
A dot plot would require intervals like the histogram uses, so it would not actually simplify or improve the way the data is shown to viewers.
hints: Count the total number of data values represented by the histogram bars.
Think about how many different exact scores the students could have—if spread across a wide range with many different values, what happens to readability on a dot plot?

problemText: A data set contains these values: 10, 12, 15, 18, 20. What is the mean of this data set?
hints: Add all five values together.
Then divide your sum by how many values there are.

problemText: Four students recorded the number of books they read last month: 3, 5, 7, 9. What is the median number of books read?
hints: The values are already in order, so you do not need to rearrange them.
With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

problemText: Five friends compared how many video games they own: 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Which statement is true about the mean and median of this data set?
choices: The mean is 12 but the median is 10.
The mean is higher than the median.
The median is higher than the mean.
The mean and median are both 12.
hints: Find the mean by adding all five values and dividing by 5.
Find the median by identifying the middle value when the data is in order.

problemText: A runner recorded her mile times for seven practice runs, in minutes: 6.5, 6.8, 6.9, 7.0, 7.1, 7.2, 12.5. The last time was interrupted by a stop sign, making it much higher than her other runs. Which statement best explains why the median is a better measure of her typical mile time than the mean?
choices: The 12.5 minute run is an outlier that pulls the mean higher, but the median is only affected by the order of values, not by how extreme they are.

The median is computed by finding the middle position in an ordered list, so extreme values like 12.5 do not influence which number sits in the center the way they push the sum higher in the mean calculation.
The mean depends on adding all values together and dividing, so a single very large number like 12.5 affects the mean much more than it affects the median, which depends only on position.
The median always ignores the largest and smallest values in a dataset to focus on the middle range, whereas the mean treats every value equally regardless of how far it sits from the others.
hints: Think about what happens to the mean when one very large value is added to the sum.
Think about what the median cares about — is it the actual size of each value, or something else?

problemText: A teacher records attendance across eight class periods: 28, 29, 29, 30, 30, 31, 31, 32 students present. Calculate both the mean and the median attendance. Then decide which one better describes a typical class size, and explain why.
choices: Mean is 30, median is 30; the mean is always better at describing typical values.
Mean is 30, median is 30; either measure works well because there is no outlier pulling the data apart.
Mean is 30.25, median is 30; the median is better because it ignores the highest and lowest values.
Mean is 30.25, median is 30.5; the mean is more useful because it is larger.
hints: Add all eight values and divide by 8 to find the mean.
The two middle values (4th and 5th) average to find the median; then check whether the data is spread evenly or pulled by an outlier.

problemText: Six friends compared their test scores: 72, 75, 78, 81, 84, 91. The student who scored 91 studied harder than the others. Another student is worried that this high score will make the class average (mean) too high and not represent where most students actually performed. Is this student's concern correct? Justify your answer by calculating both the mean and the median and comparing them to the rest of the data.
choices: Yes, the concern is correct; the 91 pulls the mean up to 80.2 while the median stays at 79.5, so the mean no longer describes the typical student.
Yes, the concern is correct; whenever one score is noticeably higher than all the others, it must be an outlier that forces the mean to be unrepresentative of most students' actual performance.
No, the concern is incorrect; the mean is 80.2 and the median is 79.5, which are both close to most of the scores because 91 is not extreme enough to be an outlier here.
No, the concern is incorrect; the median is 81, which is higher than the mean of 80.2, so the high score pulls the median up more than the mean and actually makes the mean more reliable.
hints: Calculate the mean by adding all six scores and dividing by 6; calculate the median by finding the mean of the 3rd and 4th values when ordered.
An outlier must be far enough from the rest of the data to pull the mean noticeably away — look at whether 91 sits far from the other five scores or reasonably close.

problemText: A data set has a minimum value of 8, Q1 = 15, median = 20, Q3 = 28, and maximum = 40. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
hints: IQR is the spread of the middle half of the data.
Subtract the first quartile from the third quartile.

problemText: A coach records the time in seconds it takes each swimmer on the team to complete a lap: 45, 52, 38, 48, 55, 41, 50. Order the data first, then find the median of this seven-value data set.
choices: 45 seconds
50 seconds
52 seconds
48 seconds
hints: Start by arranging all seven values from smallest to largest.
The median is the middle value when the data is ordered.

problemText: Two sixth-grade classes took a spelling test. Class A had a mean score of 82 and a range of 18. Class B had a mean score of 82 and a range of 5. Both classes have the same average, but what does the range tell you about how the students performed differently?
choices: Class B's students had scores much closer to each other, while Class A's scores were more spread out.
Class A has better spellers because a larger range means more students scored very high on the test.
Class B's students all scored exactly 82 because the range of 5 means no one deviated from the mean.
The two classes performed identically in terms of consistency because both have the same mean score of 82.
hints: Range measures spread, not center. A small range means values cluster together.
Two data sets can have the same mean but very different spreads.

problemText: A art teacher collected data on how many drawings each of her eight students completed in one week: 3, 7, 5, 9, 4, 8, 6, 10. After ordering the data, find both the first quartile (Q1) and the third quartile (Q3), then calculate the interquartile range.
hints: With an even count of values, find the median of the lower half and upper half separately.
The lower half contains the four smallest values; the upper half contains the four largest values.

problemText: A manager tracks the number of online orders received each day over nine days: 12, 8, 15, 10, 14, 9, 16, 11, 13. One unusual day had only 8 orders. What is the range, and what does the interquartile range tell you about the effect of that unusual day?
choices: Range = 8; the IQR equals the range, proving the unusual day spreads the data evenly throughout.
Range = 16; the IQR should always be half the range when extreme values are present in the dataset.
Range = 8; the IQR is much smaller than the range, showing that the unusual low day barely affects the spread of the middle half of the data.
Range = 16; the IQR remains stable because it ignores extreme values and focuses only on the middle 50 percent of the data.
hints: Calculate range as maximum minus minimum. Then find Q1 and Q3 to compute the IQR.
The IQR focuses on only the middle half of the data, so extreme values have little effect on it.

problemText: Two runners tracked their mile times in minutes over six weeks: Runner A's times were 8.2, 8.0, 7.9, 8.1, 7.8, 8.3; Runner B's times were 7.5, 8.5, 7.4, 8.6, 7.3, 8.7. Both have a median of approximately 8.05 minutes. Calculate the IQR for each runner, then describe what the IQRs tell you about consistency.
choices: Runner A's IQR is 0.4 minutes and Runner B's IQR is 0.9 minutes; neither runner is consistent because both their times show some variation week to week.
Runner A's IQR is 0.3 minutes and Runner B's IQR is 1.0 minutes; Runner B is more consistent because his times span a wider range across the six weeks.
Runner A's IQR is 0.2 minutes and Runner B's IQR is 1.1 minutes; Runner B is faster because his IQR is larger than Runner A's.
Runner A's IQR is 0.2 minutes and Runner B's IQR is 1.1 minutes; Runner A is much more consistent because the middle half of his times cluster tightly.
hints: Order each data set, find Q1 and Q3, then subtract to find IQR. Remember to exclude the median itself from both halves.
A smaller IQR means the middle half of values are packed closer together, showing more consistency.

problemText: A statistical question is one that anticipates variability in the answers. Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many students are in the sixth grade at Lincoln Middle School right now?
What is the capital of France?
How many legs does a dog have?
What is the favorite color of each student in our class?
hints: Think about whether the question expects one fixed answer or many different answers from different people.
A statistical question asks about multiple members of a group, where each person or object could give a different answer.

problemText: Ms. Chen is deciding between two questions to ask her students. Question A: 'How tall is the tallest student in our class?' Question B: 'How tall is each student in our class?' Which question is statistical, and why?
choices: Question B is statistical because it asks about each student separately, so different students will have different heights.
Question A is statistical because it asks about one specific student and produces only one answer, with no variability across responses.
Neither question is statistical because height is a physical characteristic that does not vary between different measurement methods or people.
Both questions are statistical because they both involve students in the class and use numerical data.
hints: Remember that mentioning a group does not automatically make a question statistical—what matters is whether each member can give a separate, different answer.
Question A asks about one specific person (the tallest student), so it has exactly one correct answer. Question B asks each student to answer about themselves.

problemText: Jordan wrote this question: 'How many text messages did I send today?' Explain whether this is a statistical question by applying the variability test.
choices: Yes, it is statistical because text messages vary in length and students send different amounts each day.
No, it is not statistical because it asks about one person at one specific time, producing only one answer.
Yes, it is statistical because many people send text messages every day and the numbers differ across different days.
No, it is not statistical because text messages are not numerical data and cannot be counted or measured.
hints: The variability test asks: would the answers differ from person to person, object to object, or time to time?
This question names only Jordan and only one day, so it produces exactly one number—not variability.

problemText: A student has these three questions: (1) 'How many ounces of water did I drink today?' (2) 'How many ounces of water does each student in my grade drink per day?' (3) 'What is the total ounces of water all students in my grade drink per day?' Use the variability test to determine which of these are statistical questions.
choices: Questions 1 and 2 are both statistical.
Questions 2 and 3 are both statistical.
Only question 2 is statistical.
Only question 3 is statistical.
hints: Question 1 is about one person on one day—does that produce one answer or many? Question 3 asks for a single total across the entire grade—does that produce one answer or many?
A statistical question must ask about each member of a group separately so that different answers are expected from different people.

problemText: Marcus wants to know about the number of hours students spend playing video games each week. He writes: 'How many hours do students spend playing video games each week?' But his teacher says this is not quite a statistical question yet. What must Marcus change to make it statistical?
choices: Change 'hours' to 'minutes' so the question uses smaller units and becomes easier for students to answer accurately.
Ask about the total number of hours all students play combined rather than each student individually, since statistical questions focus on combined data rather than personal responses.
Ask about a different topic instead, like sports or reading, because those topics are more suitable for gathering data from groups of people.
Add a specific group to his question, such as 'students in my class' or 'students in my school,' so each student can answer separately about themselves.
hints: Right now, the question says 'students' but does not specify which students. To make it statistical, you need to name a specific group.
Once Marcus names a specific group, each student in that group will be asked separately and can give a different answer—that is when it becomes statistical.

problemText: A researcher is studying breakfast habits. She considers these four questions: (A) 'How many students in the school ate breakfast yesterday?' (B) 'Did each student in the school eat breakfast yesterday?' (C) 'How many minutes did it take the school cafeteria to serve breakfast yesterday?' (D) 'How many minutes did it take for each student to eat their breakfast yesterday?' Two of these questions are statistical. Identify which two, and for each one, briefly explain why using the variability test.
choices: Questions A and C are statistical because they both ask about large groups and involve counting or measuring outcomes.
Questions B and D are statistical because different students are expected to give different answers.
Questions C and D are statistical because they both involve measuring time in minutes and studying cafeteria procedures.
Questions A and B are statistical because they both ask yes/no questions about breakfast eaten by students in the school.
hints: Apply the variability test to each question separately. Ask yourself: would the answers differ from person to person, or is there only one answer?

Question A asks for one total count for the whole school. Question C asks about one event (cafeteria service) that happened once. But Questions B and D ask about each student separately, so different students' answers are expected to differ.
